The Slender ponyfish Equulites elongatus is a small leiognathid species common in coastal waters of the Indo-West Pacific, where it typically reaches an ultimate total length of 8.1 centimeters [Li = 8.1 centimeters]. This species is characterised by a slender, compressed body and a highly protrusible mouth, features that facilitate feeding on small zooplankton and benthic invertebrates in estuarine and neritic habitats. Sexual maturation in this species is marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence; puberty is attained at a total length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly half the maximum length. The transition from juvenile to mature adult involves significant allometric shifts in body shape, particularly in the relative size of the head and the development of reproductive organs. Field surveys conducted across multiple populations indicate that the length at first reproduction is largely consistent, though local environmental conditions may introduce minor variation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], eggs of Equulites elongatus hatch after approximately 2.7 days [ab = approximately 2.7 days], an incubation period typical of small, warm-water leiognathids with pelagic eggs. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic, subsisting entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial phase of development. The weight of these newly hatched individuals is extremely low, measured at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters noted in prior studies of this species. Yolk-sac resorption is completed within a few days after eclosion, at which point the mouth opens and the larvae commence exogenous feeding. This rapid transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition is critical for survival during the early planktonic larval phase.

At 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum wet weight attained by adult Equulites elongatus has been estimated at 7.7 grams [Wwi = 7.7 grams], a modest body mass that is consistent with the species' small size and its position within the coastal plankton-based food web. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals typically achieve a wet weight of approximately 0.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.9 grams], which corresponds closely to the body size at which gonad development is initiated. These weight estimates are derived from length-weight relationships established from a comprehensive series of specimens collected across the species' range. The relatively rapid increase in body mass from the juvenile stage to the adult stage reflects a strategy of early maturation and high reproductive investment, which is commonly observed in small, short-lived teleosts inhabiting productive coastal environments.

Reproductive output in Equulites elongatus is relatively high for a fish of its size. Field observations indicate that during the spawning season, females release approximately 24.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 24.7 eggs per day], a daily fecundity that amounts to around 9,000 eggs per year [Ri = around 9,000 eggs per year] when extrapolated over the reproductive lifespan. This high fecundity is typical of small, pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce numerous small eggs as a strategy to offset high larval mortality in the plankton. The maximum reproductive rate observed in this species is remarkable given its small body size and underscores the selective pressures favouring high fecundity in environments where early life stages face intense predation.

At 28 °C [T = 28 °C], longevity in Equulites elongatus is relatively short, with maximum lifespan recorded at 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other small leiognathid species and reflects the typical pace of life in a fast-growing, early-maturing coastal fish. Natural mortality in the wild is likely driven by predation from larger piscivorous fishes and cephalopods, as well as by oceanographic variability affecting larval survival. Senescence in this species is not well studied, but the onset of reproductive senescence typically occurs near the end of the second year, after multiple spawning seasons. The relatively short lifespan, combined with high fecundity and early maturation, places Equulites elongatus firmly within the r-selected end of the life-history continuum.

The pelagic larval phase of Equulites elongatus is a critical period during which mortality is exceptionally high, often exceeding 99 percent in natural populations. The tiny prolarvae, weighing just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] at hatching, rely on their yolk reserves before transitioning to feeding on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. Once the larval-juvenile transition occurs, the growing individuals begin to occupy shallow estuarine habitats where food availability is higher and predation risk is somewhat reduced. The combination of a rapid growth rate, early maturation, and high fecundity allows this species to sustain viable populations despite intense early mortality.
